steps: A small outgrowth, called a bud, appears on the yeast cell.
The nucleus divides by mitosis, and one daughter nucleus moves into the bud.
The bud grows and may separate from the parent cell to form a new yeast cell. Sometimes it remains attached, forming a chain of cells.
items.finalAnswer: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding: a bud grows on the parent cell, receives a daughter nucleus and forms a new cell.

steps: In fungi, spores are produced in structures called sporangia, usually present at the tips of hyphae.
When the sporangium matures, it releases the spores.
Under favourable conditions, a spore germinates and grows into a new hypha, which develops into a fungus.
items.finalAnswer: Fungi reproduce by forming spores in sporangia; the released spores germinate under favourable conditions to form new hyphae.

steps: A large number of spores can be produced, helping fungi reproduce and spread.
Spores are light and can be carried by air or other means to new places.
Their thick protective walls help them survive unfavourable conditions.
Bacterial endospores also have protective coverings that help bacteria survive unfavourable conditions, such as heat and lack of water.
items.finalAnswer: Spores are numerous, readily dispersed and protected by resistant walls, helping fungi and bacteria survive and spread.

steps: A runner is a horizontal stem that grows along the ground surface.
Roots and shoots develop at the nodes of the runner.
Each rooted node can grow into an independent plant, as in strawberry and grass.
items.finalAnswer: Runners produce new plants when roots and shoots grow from their nodes.

steps: A potato tuber is an underground stem that stores food.
The small depressions on a tuber, called eyes, are buds.
When a tuber is planted, buds in its eyes sprout and grow into shoots; roots also develop, forming a new plant.
items.finalAnswer: Potatoes reproduce vegetatively from the buds, or eyes, on their underground tubers.

steps: Advantages: Vegetative propagation is a rapid method of producing new plants.
The new plants are genetically similar to the parent and retain its desirable characters.
It is useful for plants that do not produce viable seeds.
Disadvantages: There is little or no genetic variation among the offspring.
Diseases present in the parent plant may be passed to the new plants.
items.finalAnswer: Vegetative propagation is rapid and preserves desirable characters, but produces little variation and can pass diseases to offspring.

steps: The four floral whorls, from the outermost to the innermost, are calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Calyx is made up of sepals.
Corolla is made up of petals.
Androecium is made up of stamens; each stamen consists of an anther and a filament.
Gynoecium is made up of carpels (pistils); each carpel has a stigma, style and ovary.
items.finalAnswer: The four whorls are calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens) and gynoecium (carpels or pistils).

steps: Inside the ovule, a megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis and forms four megaspores.
Three megaspores degenerate, while the remaining functional megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions to form eight nuclei.
Four nuclei move to each end of the embryo sac; one nucleus from each end moves to the centre and forms the two polar nuclei.
At the micropylar end, one of the remaining nuclei forms the egg cell; the other two form synergids.
items.finalAnswer: One functional megaspore forms an eight-nucleate embryo sac; the egg cell and two synergids lie at the micropylar end, and two polar nuclei lie in the centre.
